newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Rising cocoa trend in Africa could offset El Nino.
newsitem.headline: Rising cocoa trend in Africa could offset El Nino.

text.p: Africa's 1997/98 (Oct-Sept) cocoa crops could feel the impact of dry El Nino weather forecast for late 1997, but overall output may not be affected, a crop analyst said on Tuesday.
"The main point is the effect of a trend of rising production in Africa," UK-based analyst Robert Fish of Primary Commodities Research told Reuters by telephone.
"Rising crops are more than sufficient to offset the effect of El Ninos," he added, pointing to an increase in African harvests in 1986/87 (Oct-Sept) despite an El Nino then.
The driest recent El Nino in 1982/83 gave African crops a fairly large shock, but four subsequent El Ninos made little or no impact.
Only in 1991/92, when African output dropped by almost 13 percent, did output clearly fall as a result, he said.
Ivory Coast, the world's main producer, set a record 1.2 million tonne crop in 1995/96 before another strong year in 1996/97, with 1.06 million tonnes reported by July 1997.
London broker GNI said this week Ivory Coast's 1997/98 crop could exceed 1.2 million tonnes, suggesting a new record year.
Many crop analysts will release forecasts in August.
Fish said African production fell in 1991/92 although West Africa was generally less affected by dry El Nino weather than South America and the Far East.
"There has been a very strong upward trend in African production. Stronger than was in evidence in 1982/83," he said.
Comparisons with previous El Nino years for assessing the potential effect on crops were therefore not useful, he said.
"A strong El Nino in 1997 will not necessarily have the same impact as in the 1980s," he added.

The rate of growth of planted areas in Africa was largely unknown, which meant the precise effects of El Ninos were unclear. Many Ivorian smallholders, for example, cultivated farms of three hectares or less and data on total farm area either did not exist or were out of date.
Illicit production by migrant farmers in protected forests in Ivory Coast further complicated data collection.
British consultant Landell Mills said in a recent report that world production in 1982/83 had been cut by 200-300,000 tonnes by the effects of El Nino.

A local crop analyst said the current El Nino showed signs of being strong but, like other analysts, he expected little immediate impact in 1997/98. He and others say the mid-crop from May could be affected if the weather system hit, as forecast, in late 1997.
"There are a lot of people making a big issue out of it but they are not necessarily wrong," said Fish.
Weather analysts have said El Ninos stand a 50 percent chance of arriving in West Africa -- which is at the weaker end of the El Nino weather pattern.

El Nino is the name given to a reversal of ocean water circulation in the southern Pacific. Scientists say the phenomenon is becoming more common and can mean droughts in cocoa producing regions such as Africa, Indonesia and South America.
